description: We’re a team of curious builders turning space exploration into an interactive experience. For NASA Space Apps, we’re creating a space mission design game where players plan missions, manage limited resources, and navigate tough engineering trade-offs. Inspired by NASA science and real-world constraints, our goal is to make mission design accessible, engaging, and fun—giving everyone a chance to think like a mission planner.
summary:
Mission Architect is an educational space-mission design game born from my own curiosity. I’m Franek, a young space enthusiast. After reading books and watching videos, I wanted to explore questions that went beyond what my parents could answer. NASA’s open resources offer enormous knowledge, but finding an accessible starting point can be difficult.

I created Mission Architect to bridge that gap through play. Players choose mission goals, select spacecraft equipment, and balance mass, power, budget, and communication constraints. They simulate their designs, examine the results, and improve them—learning why engineering decisions matter instead of simply receiving a score.

The game translates complex space-engineering concepts into approachable choices using simplified educational models. My goal is to help young explorers move from learning about space to thinking like mission designers. I am the lead developer, designer, and creator; my father, Michał, supports me as a helper, tester, and reviewer.
details:
Why I created Mission Architect?

My name is Franek, and I am a young space enthusiast. I love learning about space, but books and videos eventually left me with questions my parents could no longer answer. NASA’s open resources contain an enormous amount of knowledge—but exploring them can feel like drinking from a firehose.

I created Mission Architect to make the next step more accessible: a game where young explorers learn by designing their own space missions.

What the project does?

Mission Architect is an interactive space-mission design and simulation game. Players choose a scientific goal, select equipment, and balance competing engineering requirements.

The game connects individual decisions to the mission as a whole: adding an instrument is not automatically an improvement if the spacecraft cannot power it or transmit its data back to Earth.

How it works?

Players follow a repeatable learning cycle: design → simulate → review → improve.
They can:
- Select instruments and explore their suitability for mission objectives.
- Balance mass, power, budget, and communication constraints.
- Examine mission results and identify weaknesses.
- Change their design and test the consequences.
- Explore the relationships between launch, space, ground, and user segments.

Career mode provides progression, while Free Design supports experimentation. Team Room enables collaborative design, and Hall of Fame lets players compare mission results.

Our approach to learning

The project uses simplified educational models to make space-engineering concepts understandable. It is not professional flight-planning software. Its purpose is to help players develop intuition about systems, constraints, and trade-offs.

NASA’s publicly available mission-design resources provide a foundation for connecting gameplay with real space-engineering ideas. The game aims to make this knowledge approachable, rather than reproduce the complexity of
professional tools.

Challenges

The hardest challenge was making the game simple without losing the science. Feedback needed to explain why a design struggled—not merely display a score. Another challenge was showing how decisions interact: better scientific equipment may also require more power, greater mass, or stronger communications.

Team

I, Franciszek Kosmowski, am the lead developer, designer, and creator. My father, Michał Kosmowski, supports the project as a helper, tester, and reviewer.
